attributes.label: IenW
attributes.interest: A reachable country with strong dikes, where people stay safe and get from A to B, with clean air, soil and water, its living environment cared for and raw materials used sparingly. For fresh water, the goal it set with the regional governments in 2019: in 2050 the Netherlands is resilient against freshwater shortage.
attributes.influence: Responsible for national water policy, the safety, quality and availability of water among it, and for the working of Dutch water management as a whole; manages the main water system, the large rivers, lakes and seas, with Rijkswaterstaat carrying it out; may instruct provinces and water boards on regional water management where international obligations or interests beyond a region require it. Its freshwater policy ranks the uses of water in a shortage by the verdringingsreeks, which every water manager follows: agriculture in the last of its four categories, temporary irrigation of capital-intensive crops one higher. Its minister coordinates the Delta Programme for Fresh Water, which the six freshwater regions carry out, and manages the Delta Fund, which pays all of Rijkswaterstaat's freshwater measures in the main water system and 25% of a region's (up to 50% for innovative ones or those of several regions): just over €58 million for fresh water in 2026; early in 2027 the Rijk and the regions set the measures for 2028–2033. The Delta Programme 2027, which its minister presents to parliament with the Delta Fund's budget, proposes for the south-west delta that the areas with no supply from outside speed up their way to self-sufficiency, with no extra demand on the Hollandsch Diep and Haringvliet. Score 2: it shapes the island's adaptation through the province, the water board and Rijkswaterstaat; no source read shows the Delta Fund paying for a measure on the island.
attributes.affected: Drought brings freshwater shortages its policy must answer, measured nationally: in the Algemene Rekenkamer's report (2026), the 2018 drought did €450 million to €2.08 billion of economic damage in the Netherlands (Ecorys, 2019), and in the KNMI's scenarios an extremely dry summer of today is an average summer by 2050. The Rekenkamer finds that the Delta Programme for Fresh Water, which IenW's minister coordinates, has no concrete, measurable goal, so whether it is on schedule for 2050 cannot be judged; nearly three quarters of the measures studied ran 2.4 to 3 years late, and the first phase's spending, €512.5 million, came 40% above the €364.7 million estimated; while measures are delayed, the damage of drought persists. In the cabinet's reaction to the Delta Programme 2027, the Netherlands had a considerable water shortage in the summer of 2026, raised on 16 July to drought level 2, an actual water shortage: no social disruption, but damage and hindrance, with several functions and interests under pressure. No source read shows how salinisation on the island affects IenW.

attributes.label: Rijkswaterstaat
attributes.interest: A safe, liveable and reachable Netherlands, worked on together with others; in drought, the little fresh water of the large rivers and lakes divided as well as it can among all who use it.
attributes.influence: Manages the main water system for IenW, the large rivers, lakes and seas, the Delta waters outside the island's dikes among them, for national safety and fresh water supply. In drought it judges, as the water board does for its waters, whether water runs short, and divides the fresh water of the Rhine and Meuse through weirs, pumping stations and sluices by the verdringingsreeks. Most of Zeeland lies outside the area it can supply, where users depend on rain and groundwater; the island has no fresh water supplied from outside (the municipality, 2023). A pipeline to the island, which the province had explored (2021), would draw on waters it manages: the Volkerak-Zoommeer, at the Noorder Krammer or the Schelde-Rijnkanaal, or the Haringvliet, the study's most future-proof source. With LVVN, IenW and STOWA it had a knowledge programme on salt in agriculture, nature and water management drawn up (2025). Score 2: it shapes the island's adaptation indirectly, through what a supply route could draw on; none exists.
attributes.affected: Drought and salinisation fall on the main water system it manages: the fresh flow of its rivers keeps sea water from pressing too far into the country, and as the summer precipitation deficit grows, the possibility of supplying fresh water through the large rivers shrinks (IPLO, 2025). The Algemene Rekenkamer (2026) expects lower river discharges, above all in summer, more and more often, so shipping suffers drought damage more often, and a growing demand for extra flushing against salinisation; at low water levels ships sail with less load, cargo is spread over more ships and waits at the locks grow longer. When less water is available than is needed, it must divide the little fresh water there is by the verdringingsreeks. The Rekenkamer recommends that IenW's minister commission it explicitly as the executor of the Delta Programme's measures in the main water system. No source read shows how salinisation on the island affects Rijkswaterstaat, which supplies no water there.

attributes.label: Delta Climate Center
attributes.interest: Regional transitions towards sustainable, climate-resilient and prosperous deltas, in Zeeland and worldwide, with Zeeland as its living lab.
attributes.influence: A partnership of six knowledge institutes, Scalda, HZ University of Applied Sciences, University College Roosevelt, NIOZ, Utrecht University and Wageningen University & Research, at the Kenniswerf in Vlissingen, which started in mid-2023 with a budget of €88 million from the national government and the province, part of the national compensation package Wind in de Zeilen. Its themes for the Zeeland delta are sustainable food, water safety and water availability, and circularity, with three iconic projects from 2024: Delta Protein, the protein transition, mainly marine; Flexible Deltas, flood-defence landscapes that also offer a future for agriculture, salinisation and freshwater availability among their challenges, with living labs on the Westerschelde, the Oosterschelde (from the second half of 2025) and the coastal zone; and ProceZ. Score 1: no source read shows it working on Schouwen-Duiveland or with the island's farmers.
attributes.affected: In its own words, sea level rise, salinisation and drought are among the consequences of climate change noticeable in delta areas such as Zeeland, and it develops knowledge and innovations to keep them safe and flourishing. In its project Flexible Deltas, salinisation and freshwater availability are among the challenges of the polders behind the dikes, beside water safety, ecological functions and economic interests, which call for an integrated approach. Measured for Zeeland and the Southwest Delta: no source read shows how salinisation on the island, or its farms' adaptation, affects the DCC.

attributes.label: Deltares
attributes.interest: Applied research on water and the subsurface, for future, sustainable and safe deltas and a resilient infrastructure.
attributes.influence: An independent knowledge institute for applied research on water and the subsurface, working with governments, companies, knowledge institutions, universities and NGOs in the Netherlands and abroad. On the island it carried out, with KWR, Acacia Water, Agrarisch Schouwen-Duiveland and the municipality, the Living Lab's project Samenwerken voor Zoet Water (2020–2022), paid by the EU's rural development fund, the province and the municipality, whose quickscans gave 13 farmers advice on storing fresh water in the subsoil that fits the farm's soil, groundwater and economics, followed by five feasibility studies for groups of farms; drainage and infiltration, it concludes, can store far more fresh water underground than was thought; it wrote the project's final report for the municipality with KWR, Acacia Water and Buro Waterfront. With Acacia Water, Delphy, the trial farm Rusthoeve and the municipality it had anti-salinisation and double drainage on the low-lying poelgronden of three farms, at Kerkwerve and Dreischor, demonstrated and monitored (drains laid in 2022, closing meeting in 2024), half paid by the EU; with KWR and WUR it carried out LN2050, research on a climate- and water-robust layout of the countryside towards 2050, the island one of its three example areas, for its farmers, ZLTO's island branch and the Zeeland governments, part of the Ministry of Economic Affairs' Knowledge and Innovation Agenda; in 2025 it was among the knowledge institutes carrying out the national knowledge programme on salt. Score 3: the project's advice reached the participating farms directly; no source read says which partner wrote which advice.
attributes.affected: Salinisation raises knowledge questions it is among those answering: in 2025 it was among the knowledge institutes carrying out the national programme on dealing with salt in agriculture, nature and water management, which LVVN, IenW, Rijkswaterstaat and STOWA had drawn up because the growing salinisation of water and soil, partly through climate change, raises such questions, to fill fundamental gaps in knowledge, how salty the soil moisture becomes and how salt-tolerant crops are under Dutch conditions, and to make the answers usable in practice in models and tools; €400,000 was available for 2025, and the partners intend to find about €1 million a year for the whole multi-year programme (IPLO, 2025). On the island, the report it wrote with KWR and Acacia Water (Kaandorp et al., 2022) finds the farms' hesitation to invest working both ways: as long as the measures' costs, risks and gain in yield stay uncertain, farmers do not invest, and as long as they do not invest, the techniques are not refined, nothing is learned from building them, their effects cannot be monitored, and no knowledge base forms at agricultural advisory firms and contractors with which the cost of advice and building could fall; it recommends pilots with monitoring, and more research on the measures' economic feasibility. Following the report, it took part in drainage demonstrations on three of the island's farms (2022–2024). The EU paid half of their cost and the province and the municipality a large part, beside an own contribution from the participating knowledge parties.

attributes.label: Delphy
attributes.interest: Healthy, successful and sustainable cultivation: better performance for growers, through research, data-driven crop management, advice and training.
attributes.influence: A knowledge company, part of Peterson Solutions, with more than 250 professionals active in over 60 countries and its address in Wageningen; its crop experts advise growers in every plant sector, arable farming among them. It is a practice partner of the Living Lab, its manager for arable farming and field vegetables in the south-west and two soil and water experts among the partners, and with Acacia Water, Deltares, the trial farm Rusthoeve and the municipality it had anti-salinisation and double drainage on the low-lying poelgronden of three farms, at Kerkwerve and Dreischor, demonstrated and monitored (drains laid in 2022, closing meeting in 2024), half paid by the EU. In 2023 it carried out the study of the island's freshwater demand, commissioned by Droogte Oplossingen Regio Schouwen Duiveland in its own account and by ZLTO in Omroep Zeeland's: farming on the island becomes impossible without more fresh water, since the current freshwater measures and innovations supply too little, fit only part of the island, are costly and have not yet proven their value, so a supply of fresh water stays needed and more rain must be stored; ZLTO's island branch draws from it that a supply of fresh water is unavoidable. Score 2: the demonstrations give data on the techniques' effects, and its study informs the island's debate on fresh water; no source read shows it advising individual farms.
attributes.affected: It took part in drainage demonstrations on three of the island's farms (2022–2024). The EU paid half of their cost and the province and the municipality a large part, beside an own contribution from the participating knowledge parties. attributes.description: Summers with less rain and more evaporation lower the year's rain surplus, which is what recharges the lens. In a model of a drained field over saline seepage, built from measurements on the island, the recharge is each day's rain minus evaporation: in the year it used, summer evaporation (440 mm) outweighed summer rain (425 mm), so the winter did the recharging, and a smaller surplus gave a thinner lens (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3665, 3671, 3674). Within the year.
attributes.sources: de Louw, P. G. B., Eeman, S., Siemon, B., Voortman, B. R., Gunnink, J., van Baaren, E. S., & Oude Essink, G. H. P. (2011). Shallow rainwater lenses in deltaic areas with saline seepage. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, 15(12), 3659–3678. https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-15-3659-2011

attributes.description: A higher sea raises the water pressure in the sand below the clay, so more salt groundwater seeps up and the ditches get saltier; in the fields the drains will probably catch most of the effect (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 11, for Schouwen-Duiveland). The rise in pressure fades quickly with distance from the coast (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3674): in a model of the western Netherlands around Amsterdam, The Hague, Rotterdam and Utrecht, it reached up to 10 km from the coast and the main rivers, and 5 km inland it was about 40% of the rise (Oude Essink et al., 2010, pp. 3, 9). How much of the rise reaches the dikes along the Grevelingen, which has no tide, the sources read do not say. Within the year: the seepage follows the water pressures, which change constantly (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3675).

attributes.description: More winter rain raises the winter's rain surplus, which recharges the lens. In a model of a drained field over saline seepage, built from measurements on the island, the recharge is each day's rain minus evaporation, and from October to March of the year it used 397 mm of rain fell against 108 mm of evaporation (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3665). Kaandorp et al. (2022, p. 11) expect the changing rain to raise the island's winter groundwater levels in part. Within the year.

attributes.description: More winter rain gives the drains more to carry off: tile drains discharge the shallow groundwater quickly during each rain (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3661, measured on the island), and on Schouwen-Duiveland enough rain falls over the year, but a large part of it is drained away in the wet season (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 54). Within the year.

attributes.description: Rainwater infiltration builds up the floating freshwater lens, but slowly: the lens is a stock that a year's recharge barely moves. In a model of a drained field over saline seepage, built from measurements on the island, the centre of the mixing zone moves at most 0.1 m in a year as the recharge swings with the seasons, the vertical flow at most 1.2 mm a day, and every run settled from saline groundwater to a stationary lens within 30 years (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3665, 3673). So a change in recharge takes years to show in the lens.

attributes.description: Where the lens is thin, saline groundwater lies just below the roots and reaches the root zone by capillary rise. In the island's low polders with saline seepage the lens is about 2 m thick, its mixing zone in the clay top layer, and capillary rise of saline groundwater is very likely now, possibly damaging crops (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3660, 3662, 3667, 3673, 3675, measured on Schouwen-Duiveland); the topsoil there is fresh thanks to the rainwater lens, which makes farming possible, and these low polders of heavy clay make up a large part of the island (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 4, 10). On Duiveland the salt water reaches into or almost into the root zone in places (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 26). Within the year: in a dry season, with the groundwater below the drains, the flow there is only upward (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3673).

attributes.description: The thinner the lens under the well, the sooner the salt below reaches it: in the Freshmaker pilot at Ovezande, Zuid-Beveland, the pumped water grew saltier late in each pumping season, which the report explains by the lens thinning as fresh water is pumped, so that upconing could reach the shallow well (Oude Essink et al., 2018, p. 67). Zeeland allows wells only where the fresh groundwater is more than 15 m thick (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 26). Measured on a creek ridge elsewhere in Zeeland, a lens like those under the island's creek ridges (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10). Within the year.

attributes.description: Holds in the low polders, where the thin rainwater lens keeps the topsoil fresh, which makes farming possible there (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10, for the island): water a measure keeps in the lens reaches only the crop on that field, as groundwater and soil moisture, and lies too deep for its roots at germination (p. 33), when most of the island's shortfall falls (pp. 27, 31); later in the summer the soil supplies a well-established crop (p. 27). The lens under the creek ridges and the dunes reaches crops only through wells (pp. 26, 38), which is Groundwater extraction for irrigation → Freshwater availability for crops. Within the season.

attributes.description: Peat oxidation and clay settling lower the land surface relative to NAP at millimetres a year, so a decimetre takes decades: Dutch land below sea level is still subsiding up to 1 m per century, fastest in peat areas (Oude Essink et al., 2010, pp. 1, 3, 8–9). A rate for Schouwen-Duiveland's clay polders is not yet sourced.

attributes.description: The lower a polder lies, the more salt groundwater seeps up into it: on the island the eastern polders lie somewhat higher than the western ones and so have no or far less seepage pressure (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 28), and comparing the island's elevation with a regional groundwater model, seepage occurs in the polders below sea level and rain soaks in on the dunes, the creek ridges and the polders above it, the two strongly correlated (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3661, 3673). Drainage depth is measured from the surface, so at the same depth a lower polder holds its ditch level lower, which lowers the counter-pressure on the salt groundwater (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 37). Within the year: the seepage follows the water pressures (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3675).

attributes.description: Salt in the root zone puts sodium (Na+) on the clay in place of calcium (Ca2+); once fresh water washes the salt out, clay that holds much sodium disperses: its aggregates and pores collapse, with troubles to be expected above 1 m.e. of exchangeable sodium per 100 g of dry soil. The delay is on the way back: structure collapses within the first winter after the salt leaches out, but the clay only recovers as calcium replaces the sodium again, about 0.7 m.e. Na per 100 g a year in the top 10 cm of soil with calcium carbonate, which takes 5 to 10 years on heavy clay and about a year on light soil, while soil without it is expected to recover more slowly (van Beekom et al., 1953b, pp. 225–228, after the 1945 and 1953 floods in Zeeland). Seawater flooding is a much larger salt dose than seepage; soils that took up less sodium recover faster, and no source read shows how much sodium the island's seepage puts on its clay.
attributes.simplification: Folds Sodium on the clay, a stock between the two: the salt puts sodium on the clay, and the sodium breaks the clay's structure once the salt washes out. The sign is the product of the two steps (+, then −), so no loop through the link changes, and the stock's slowness is the link's delay. What one link distorts: the delay lies on the way back only, the structure collapsing within the first winter after the salt leaches out and recovering over years, while the link draws one delay for both ways.
attributes.sources: van Beekom, C. W. C., van den Berg, C., de Boer, Th. A., van der Molen, W. H., Verhoeven, B., Westerhof, J. J., & Zuur, A. J. (1953b). Reclaiming land flooded with salt water: II. Exchangeable cations. Netherlands Journal of Agricultural Science, 1(4), 225–244. https://library.wur.nl/ojs/index.php/njas/article/view/17860

attributes.description: Upward saline seepage keeps the rainwater lens thin: the larger the seepage flux, the higher the lens's mixing zone, and in the island's seepage areas the lens is mostly under 2 m, its mixing zone in the clay top layer (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3660, 3673–3675, measured on the island; Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10). Years, so a delay: in a model of a drained field over saline seepage, built from measurements on the island, every run settled to a stationary lens within 30 years (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3665).

attributes.description: Rain recharges the lens only once it has soaked into the soil. Before the floods, Zeeland's well-drained clay let the winter's rain surplus soak through almost completely; once sodium had broken down the structure of the topsoil, it became impervious and sticky when wet, part of the rain ran off over the surface and pools stood on the land, the more so the heavier the clay (van Beekom et al., 1953a, p. 157; 1953b, p. 233, measured in the flooded polders of Zeeland, by R1's own mechanism). Within the year: the structure a soil has in a winter sets how much of that winter's rain soaks in. Whether what soaks in reaches the lens or leaves through the drains is set by the drainage depth and the seepage (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3674).

attributes.description: A seedbed in soil with its structure lets the crops germinate better, with less resowing, and yields rise, most for crops sensitive to structure: on flooded clay in Zeeland, plots whose structure gypsum restored yielded up to 15% more sugar beet, 8% more onions and, on heavy clay, up to twice the summer barley, while cereals on light soil gained little (van Beekom et al., 1953b, p. 234, Table 9). Part of the gain is the longer time to work the soil, the link through Spring workability of the fields. Within the year.

attributes.description: Fresh water supplied from outside adds to what crops can draw on: the island's farming depends on the rain that falls and is stored in the root zone or underground, and none is brought in (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 4), which leaves farms short of water in dry periods (p. 8). Within the season.

attributes.description: Active infiltration adds winter water to the lens, on the creek ridges, the dunes and where a sand layer lies under the clay: the creek-ridge infiltration system raises the groundwater through the drains in winter so the lens grows, and the Freshmaker and underground storage inject winter water through a deep drain or a well, all to pump in summer (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 20–22, 38, for the island). What limits it on most of the island is fresh water to infiltrate, since the surface water is mostly saline and drain water the likeliest source (pp. 38, 43, 55), and the permit (pp. 26, 45). Years to a decade, so a delay: on the island's own creek ridge, infiltration with controlled drainage added about 60,000 m³ of fresh water under a 9.5-ha field in ten years and thickened the lens by up to 3.5 m (p. 44, a groundwater model of 2020–2050); under a creek ridge on Walcheren, raising the winter water table 0.5 m thickened a 13–15 m lens by 6–8 m in ten years, and the lens had not reached its new thickness yet (Pauw et al., 2015, pp. 1424–1425, 1429, a model result, which transfers since the island's sandy creek ridges also take in rain over saline groundwater: de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3673).

attributes.description: What farmers pump beyond what the rain puts back thins the lens, the boundary with the saline groundwater below rising: the water board's limit of 800 m³ per hectare a year rests on the balance between recharge by rain, irrigation water and extraction, set to keep the fresh groundwater in stock and the fresh-salt boundary from rising (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b), and pumping too fast risks salinisation (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 20–21). Within those rules the effects are meant to stay within the farm's field, with in principle no depletion, and Deltares's modelling of the rules (2018) found them generally enough to prevent strong salinisation under and around the well (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021, for Zeeland). How fast the lens responds to pumping, no source read shows.

attributes.description: The more a well pumps from the lens, the further salt groundwater rises towards it: in the Freshmaker pilot at Ovezande, Zuid-Beveland, the water pumped from the shallow well grew saltier as each pumping season went on (Oude Essink et al., 2018, p. 67). The report on the island's freshwater measures lists salinisation at too high a pumping rate as a risk of the creek-ridge infiltration system and of underground storage (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 20–21). Within the year: the cone follows the season's pumping.

attributes.description: A larger harvest per hectare raises income at a given price, the price being World prices of conventional crops. The + holds in full where only the island's yield falls, to salt or a local shortage of fresh water. A dry summer across north-west Europe also raises the price, since the harvests there set it: for potatoes, north-west Europe is one market, and their price was highest in the extremely dry 2018 (Janssens et al., 2020, p. 8). Then what a farm loses depends on how it sells: in 2018, higher prices could help onion growers make up for a harvest forecast 44% below the year before, while potato growers mostly held contracts at prices agreed in advance (NOS, 2018), some 80% of the crop at around nine cents a kilo while free-market potatoes reached 30 (DutchNews.nl, 2018); onions are rarely sold under such contracts (Bogosavac, 2018). On the island, a farm with its own stored water gains from the high prices of a dry year (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 36). Within the year, as the harvest is sold.

attributes.description: A fall in the land's value that has happened, through salt in R8: does a farm whose land lost value object harder to the next plan? Through its solvency, yes (−); where compensation pays more than the land would fetch on the market, the concern may fall instead (+). A hypothesis for the group model building session, with both signs as the question to farmers.
attributes.simplification: Folds Owners' concern about their land's value, which gathered the reasons for objecting: a fall in the land's value, and a plan that would lower it, raised landowning farmers' concern, and the concern raised their objections. The sign is the product of the two steps, so R8 keeps its polarity, and the concern was no actor's decision of its own. A tenant's concern, losing the lease, was never part of it. What it leaves out: why owners object is no variable on the drawing, a question for the group model building session.

attributes.description: With the same debt, a lower land value is a higher debt relative to the farm's assets: land is 70% of an arable farm's balance sheet (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 13), and its rise in value is what made arable farms' solvency 81% in 2018 (p. 21). A high solvency can let a farm borrow more and at a lower rate (p. 19); the debt itself does not shrink when the land loses value. It holds for the land a farm owns: farms owning little of it barely gain from a rising price (p. 26). Within the year: the farm accounts value the land each year (p. 13).
attributes.sources: van der Meulen, H., van der Meer, R., & van Asseldonk, M. (2020). Financiering transitie naar duurzame landbouw: Inzicht in het huidige financieringslandschap en ontwikkelingen (Rapport 2020-097). Wageningen Economic Research. https://edepot.wur.nl/532092

attributes.description: Stricter capital rules raise what a bank charges for a loan: for every loan a bank must hold capital, as the law on banks' solvency sets, the more the higher the credit risk, and the cost of that capital, the return its shareholders require, is part of the interest each client pays (ABN AMRO, n.d.-a). The final Basel III standards raise that capital, EU banks' minimum Tier 1 capital requirement by an estimated 9.0% at full implementation in 2028 (European Banking Authority, 2023). Measured across EU banks: no source read gives the change for Dutch farm loans. Within the year: the bank prices the capital with each loan.

attributes.description: Potatoes and onions are planted and sown in spring, and their soil work must not be done when the soil is too wet, which smears and compacts it and keeps an onion seedbed from forming; a potato crop is best planted early where the soil allows (Verstand et al., 2021, pp. 25, 27, from the Dutch cultivation guides). So the more of the rotation they take, the more farmers need fields that dry early in spring, which holding water back makes hard for farmers who want onto the land with heavy machinery (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021c, p. 44); on Duiveland the board moves to the higher summer level in March and April as the soil work allows (2021a, p. 66). No source read shows how much spring soil work the new crops need: the sign rests on their needing less. Within the year.

attributes.description: A farm that relies on high margins can give fewer hectares to lower-margin new crops.

More income from the land raises what buyers bid for it, through what they expect an extra hectare to earn an expanding farm over the years of the investment rather than through last year's income (Farjon et al., 2013, p. 2; Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, pp. 2–3). The + holds beside drivers the island's farms cannot move: since 1970 the Dutch price has risen tenfold while net value added rose two- to threefold, carried by scale enlargement and falling interest rates (Farjon et al., 2013, pp. 1–2). Across individual land transactions in the Netherlands from 2004 to 2011, the expected revenue from the land had a significant positive effect on the price, beside land regulations, the spatial environment and local market conditions (Boere, 2015, pp. 81, 98). Years: the price follows expected income, and its swings ran over years, falling by half in real terms in the late 1970s and by 30% between 1995 and 2005 (p. 2): a delay.

attributes.description: More income leaves more, after the household's spending and the farm's payment obligations, repayments included, to save for investment; a negative income leaves too little to reserve, and machines then age (Verhagen et al., 2018, pp. 23, 25). Within the year: income adds to the savings in the year it is earned.

attributes.description: Capacity to invest decides whether a farm can pay for a storage measure, not whether it wants to.

Capacity to invest decides whether a farm can pay for the switch (new machines, the first years of a new crop), not whether it wants to. The costs of salt-tolerant seed and soil amendments may not make up for the yield and income salt takes in the first years, when setting up costs most, and the benefits are not always obvious in the short term (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 60); farms whose financial buffers shrink are expected to invest less, slowing their modernisation and sustainability, and banks often count financing a new concept whose returns are not yet proven as a risk (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 6). Within the year: the crop is chosen each season.

attributes.description: Higher temperatures and drier weather raise evapotranspiration, the water crops use when they have enough, highest in sunny, warm and dry weather (Allen et al., 1998, FAO-56). Once a crop has drawn the root zone down beyond the water it can take up easily, it uses less water than it needs, in proportion to what is left in the root zone (Allen et al., 1998, ch. 8): the shortfall is the part of the demand that rain, soil moisture and irrigation leave unmet, so the more the crops need, the larger it is. On Schouwen-Duiveland's clay a crop that has come up well gets through the summer on the soil's good supply of moisture, so the shortfall falls mostly at germination early in the season, when a small gift of about 20 mm would cover it; onions also need water while they grow (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 27, 31, 38, from talks with the island's farmers). Within the year.
attributes.simplification: Folds Crop water demand, a step between the two with no actor and no decision: hotter, drier summers raise what crops need, and what they need beyond the water they get is the shortfall. The sign is the product of the two steps (+, then +). Hotter, drier summers is a Constant, so no loop runs through the link. What it leaves out: what crops need is no variable of its own, so a crop's own water need, new crops against the current ones, cannot enter; no source read shows whether the new crops need less.

attributes.description: Rain, irrigation and capillary rise from the groundwater add water to the root zone and lower its depletion; once the depletion passes the readily available water, the crop uses less water than it needs (Allen et al., 1998, FAO-56 ch. 8, eqs. 84–85, a daily water balance). So the more fresh water crops can draw on, the smaller the shortfall, within the season. On the island's farms a gift of 20 to 25 mm at germination makes the difference where none can be given now (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 27, 55).

attributes.description: Farmers pump more fresh groundwater as the shortfall grows: the water board registered a considerable increase in extractions in recent years, which the more extreme drought certainly influenced, so the volume pumped rises in dry years (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021, for Zeeland, whose farms pump under the same rules as the island's). On Schouwen-Duiveland the farms get their fresh water from rain and from the fresh groundwater; the shallow groundwater and the ditches are brackish to salt, and no water can be brought in (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 8). They may pump only from fresh groundwater more than 15 m thick, under the creek ridges and the dunes (p. 26): in the low polders the farmers talked to do not irrigate, while on a creek ridge a livestock farmer pumps from two deep drains for grassland through the summer, and an arable farmer irrigates about 20 mm at germination, the report not saying where that water comes from (pp. 27–28, 40, 43). So the link runs where a farm has fresh groundwater under it. Within the year.

attributes.description: What farmers pump is fresh water their crops get: what pumping gains them. On the island it goes onto the field by reel sprinkler or by drip, and the method sets how much of it the crop gets: drip loses less water, so a cubic metre covers more land, while a reel usually gives several gifts per hectare (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 35, in its cost-benefit analysis for the island's farms). On a cluster of three farms on a creek ridge, a livestock farmer irrigates grassland in dry years, in midsummer too, from two deep drains under a permit of up to 16,000 m³ a year (pp. 40, 43). The salt a well may draw up with the water runs through Upconing of salt groundwater. Within the season: within the year, no delay.

attributes.description: A crop that uses less water than it needs yields less, in proportion: its relative yield falls by a crop's yield response factor times its relative shortfall in evapotranspiration, over the season 1.1 for potatoes and onions, 1.0 for sugar beet and 1.05 for winter wheat, the loss small in the vegetative and ripening periods and large in flowering and yield formation (Allen et al., 1998, FAO-56 ch. 8, eq. 90 and Table 24, after FAO paper 33, general). On the island, farmers in the western low polders find the shortfall falls mostly at germination, and a crop that emerged well loses little to drought later in the summer (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 27); a potato grower at Nieuwerkerk lost a fifth of his 2026 harvest, the potatoes smaller too, when growth stopped in the June heat and the rain came too late, his ditch water too saline to irrigate from (van Essen, 2026). Within the season.

In the cost study for the island's farms, one irrigation gift of 20–25 mm by reel costs about €200, and surface drip irrigation €1,000 a hectare (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 35), figures the study takes from earlier work, not measured on the island. attributes.description: Dry summers lower the discharge of the great rivers, and drought more often brings a water shortage, in which the scarce water is divided among drinking water, nature, agriculture and shipping (KNMI, 2023, p. 42, the Planbureau voor de Leefomgeving's risks for the Netherlands, measured nationally): a route can only carry what summer discharge and the national distribution in drought (the verdringingsreeks, IenW and Rijkswaterstaat) leave for the region, outside the CLD's scale. Within the year: a summer's discharge sets that summer's supply.
attributes.simplification: Folds Fresh water available for supply in drought: dry summers leave less river water for a supply route, and the route carries what is left. The sign is the product of the two steps (−, then +). Hotter, drier summers is a Constant, so no loop runs through the link. What it leaves out: the river water left for the region in drought, which the national distribution decides outside the CLD's scale, is no variable of its own.

No delay drawn: how quickly a dry summer turns into a call, no source read shows.

attributes.description: The body deciding on a route weighs the call; so far a study has followed and no route has been decided on (Freshwater supply route to the island). Years, so a delay: a route has to be decided on, paid for and built.

Clay that has lost its structure stays wet long into spring, so it can be worked only late and the time to make a seedbed is very short; restored with gypsum, it dries sooner and can be worked for a longer period (van Beekom et al., 1953b, pp. 233–234, on clay in Zeeland, Schouwen-Duiveland among it, flooded by the sea in 1944–45, the sodium breaking down the structure as in Clay dispersion & sodification). Within the year.

attributes.description: The deeper the ditch levels lie below the fields, the sooner the fields drain and dry after rain. By the water board's rules for its whole area, the drooglegging is set at an optimum for each use and soil, against both wet and drought damage (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 7); at half the design discharge it must keep a field's drains, laid at their optimal depth, all but above the ditch water (p. 8); and an area 10 cm or more short of its optimum counts as too wet (p. 9). On Duiveland four level areas may run a lower target for a while in wet periods, where the fields' drainage and workability need it (2021a, p. 40), and the move from the winter to the summer level in spring follows the farmers' soil work (p. 66). Within the season, no delay.

attributes.description: Fields that cannot be worked in time are planted late: a later planting date can shorten the potato's growing season, since later in the season it is often too wet to harvest, and where blight cannot be controlled, as in organic farming, it costs yield, so an early date is preferred where the soil allows (Verstand et al., 2021, p. 25, from the Dutch cultivation guides, for the Netherlands). No source read shows it for onions or sugar beet. Within the year.

attributes.description: Where fields stay too wet to work, farmers want lower ditch levels: what deep drainage gains them. In the water board's words, holding water back longer as a buffer for dry times is sometimes hard for farmers who want onto the land with heavy machinery (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021c, p. 44, its management programme for its whole area): the board's account of the farmers' interest, not the farmers' own. No source read shows how much a wet spring raises the demand. Within the year.

attributes.description: The deeper the ditch levels lie below the fields, the more peat lies above the groundwater, where it compacts and oxidises, so the land falls faster: by the water board's rules for its whole area, peat soil above the groundwater subsides in response to drainage, and where the soil is prone to settling the board changes levels with restraint to limit it (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 13). On the island it holds Schouwen's summer levels high on purpose to limit subsidence by peat compaction, which leaves the salt-marsh soils between too little drainage depth (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, p. 45), and changes a level in soil prone to settling by no more than the land has subsided since (p. 50); Duiveland's plan changed levels with great care where peat lies below (2021a, p. 67). Within the year: the board weighs the risk by the summer groundwater level against the ditch level and the depth of the peat (2021b, p. 50). No source read gives how much faster the land falls per decimetre of drainage.

attributes.description: Lower ditch levels lower the counter-pressure on the salt groundwater, so the seepage pressure rises; a higher level lowers it (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 37, the board's analysis for Duiveland's water level plan). The seepage is driven by the higher water pressure in the sand below the polders' clay (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10). Within the year: the water pressures in the top layer change constantly with recharge and drainage (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3675).

attributes.description: The board holds the ditch levels lower in winter than in summer to prevent water damage in winter, and a higher winter level would keep the groundwater from sinking as deep (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 37, its analysis for Duiveland): the deeper the ditches stand in winter, the more of the rain they and the drains carry off. On a creek ridge studied for water storage, where the winter depth is over 1.5 m in large parts, the drains and ditches carry the excess rain off fast, and a higher winter level might raise the groundwater and with it the recharge (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 42–43). Within the year.

attributes.description: A water level plan sets the levels the board pursues and maintains (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021d, 2022), after its procedure: the executive board adopts a draft, open to views for six weeks; the general board adopts the plan; appeal is open for six weeks (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 17–18), for Duiveland from February to August 2021 (2021a, p. 53; 2021d). Its levels take effect once the works they need are in place (2025, p. 18): Duiveland's plan proposed studying a raise in 14 level areas, most possible only once the discharge capacity is enlarged (2021a, p. 69), and the works for that were still being put to the island in March 2026 (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026a). Years, so a delay.

attributes.description: The water board weighs farmers' need for low levels against raising them: it involves farming among the interest groups as it prepares a plan and weighs their input (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 17), and on Duiveland moves to the higher summer level in March and April as the farmers' soil work allows (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 66). How much the farmers' views weigh against the board's other aims, no source read shows: on Duiveland four views against a raise the plan proposed to study did not change the plan (p. 53). Years, so a delay: the board weighs it as it prepares a plan, which it does when its evaluation every three years, weighing among other things the reports of those concerned, finds a plan no longer current, or once a plan is 17 years old (2025, pp. 16–17).

attributes.description: The water board names the gradually increasing salinisation a concern for the fresh water farming needs, the thin fresh groundwater lenses most threatened, and aims to keep or enlarge the lenses: by not lowering target levels much, since a lower level lowers the counter-pressure on the salt groundwater and raises the seepage pressure, while a raise lowers it (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 37, a criterion of its analysis for Duiveland's water level plan). So the more seepage salts the soil's fresh water, the more reason the board has to raise levels, the lens being what it protects (Saline seepage → Rainwater lens thickness in the low polders). On Duiveland the plan of 2021 proposed studying a raise in 14 level areas to enlarge the fresh water in the soil and give crops more moisture (p. 69); how far seepage weighed there against drought, no source read shows. Years, so a delay: the board weighs it as it prepares a plan, which it does when its evaluation every three years finds a plan no longer current, or once a plan is 17 years old (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 16–17).

attributes.description: Rising pumping costs give the water board a reason to raise the levels.

By the water board's rules, the views sent on a draft plan within six weeks are answered in the decision, anyone affected may appeal at the court for six weeks after it, and the board consults the region first so that as few conflicts as possible arise to slow or interrupt the procedure (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 17–18). So objections can delay, change or stop a plan to raise the levels while it is pending; with none pending they change nothing, and they never lower a level. On the island the views on the two plans of 2021 changed neither: Duiveland's 25 views from six people (2021a, p. 53) and Schouwen's 11 from five, which added some studies (2021b, pp. 7–8). The only views against a raise, four on Duiveland's proposed study of one, gave as their reason the concern that flooding becomes likelier in extreme rain, not the land's value (2021a, p. 53); none of Schouwen's opposed the raises in its ten level areas (2021b, pp. 7–8, 53). The region's reactions before each draft were taken into the work on it (2021a, pp. 52–53; 2021b, p. 7). Whether anyone appealed either plan, no source read shows. Elsewhere in Zeeland a view did change the same board's plan: on the raise of a winter level in the Braakman, near Terneuzen, ZLTO objected for seven farmers that one party's gain should not harm another, and the plan of 2015 took a phased raise, its first step only once the field that suffers most has been acquired and its second within six years (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2015, p. 2). Within the year, as the plan is decided.

attributes.description: Seepage that reaches the ditches is pumped out with the rain: across most of Duiveland the waterways catch salt or brackish seepage from below (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 20); Schouwen's water comes mainly from rain and partly from seepage, strongest at its edges and in the low inlagen (2021b, pp. 25–26), all of it flowing to the pumping stations (2021b, p. 24; 2021a, p. 21); and the low western polders, under seepage, drain their brackish to salt water through pumping stations (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 27). The board's electricity follows the water pumped (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026e, p. 18), so more seepage costs more, within the year. No source read gives seepage's share of the water pumped on the island.

attributes.description: The board passes its pumping costs on through its levy, part of the costs of its water management, of which unbuilt land other than nature carries 22.78% for 2026 (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026c, art. 2). One rate holds across its whole area, so a cost that rises on the island is spread over all of it: the law lets the board charge pumped areas up to 100% more (Waterschapswet, 2026, art. 122), and its ordinance for 2026 does not.

Whether a tenant pays it through the rent, no source read shows. Within the year: the levy is charged each year.

attributes.description: Once a crop's root zone salinity, as the conductivity of the saturated soil extract (ECe), passes its threshold, its yield falls in proportion to the excess (Allen et al., 1998, ch. 8, eq. 89): onions lose 16% per dS/m above 1.2 dS/m and potatoes 12% above 1.7, rated sensitive and moderately sensitive, against 5.9% above 7.0 for sugar beet and 7.1% above 6.0 for wheat (Table 23), so on the island's rotations salt takes most from potatoes and onions. The harm is osmotic at once and comes from sodium or chloride building up in the leaves more slowly (Munns & Tester, 2008, pp. 654–656). Table 23 is a guideline from experiments mostly under irrigation, tolerance varying with climate, soil and practice, and crops are often less tolerant as they germinate (Table 23, note 1): crop physiology that holds on the island's fields, its thresholds not measured there. Within the season.

attributes.description: Harvest lost to salt is income lost: at the farm, salt lowers the yield and raises the cost of inputs such as fresh water and soil amendments, and the damage salt does in the Netherlands is estimated at 577 to 610 million euro a year, most of it agricultural revenue lost to lower yields (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 12). Salt on the island's fields does not move the price, which the harvests of north-west Europe set (Janssens et al., 2020, p. 8), so a harvest lost to it is lost at that price. Within the year, as the harvest is sold.

attributes.description: A field moved from a current crop to a new salt-tolerant one no longer has a conventional harvest for salt to take: the link holds by what Harvest lost to salt counts, the fields still under the current crops. Within the year, from the next season's crop.
attributes.simplification: The new crops are taken to lose nothing to salt. That holds for crops grown on saline land, such as sea fennel and sea banana on an arable farm at Colijnsplaat (EU CAP Network, 2023), and for quinoa, among the crops better suited to saline conditions (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 63). A new crop as sensitive as the current ones loses about as much, and R6 does not run through it.

attributes.description: A salt-tolerant variety loses less of its harvest at the same salinity of the root zone: in field trials on Texel from 2012 to 2018, most potato cultivars kept 90% of their yield up to a soil salinity (ECe) of about 4 to 5 dS/m, some about twice that (van Straten et al., 2021, p. 1), Elgar and Rivola above 7.5 dS/m (p. 10). Measured on sandy soil, the salt brought by irrigation water: the sign holds on the island, since the trials relate yield to the salinity of the root zone, which drives Harvest lost to salt there whatever brings the salt; the size need not, as the authors warn for other soils and climates (p. 11).

attributes.description: A hectare moved from a high-margin current crop to a new one earns the new crop's margin instead, and the margin of protein crops cannot compete with most other crops (Polman et al., 2026, p. 9). The link holds by what the element counts, the hectares taken from the high-margin crops: the area of a minor crop depends on the room left in the rotation (Polman et al., 2026, p. 17), and in a simulation for Flanders quinoa mostly took the place of maize and winter wheat (Cloet et al., 2024, p. 3). Within the year: the crop is chosen each season.

attributes.description: A tolerant variety earns less than the variety it replaces where salt does not limit the crop: salt-tolerant varieties are usually lower yielding, high-yielding varieties being sensitive to stress through a trade-off between tolerance and yield (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 30). In greenhouse pots at Wageningen in 2024, a salt-tolerant potato variety lost 18% of its tuber weight under salt against 39% for a sensitive one (p. 21), yet on fresh water it netted about €1,800 a hectare with the soil amendment that served it best, against about €2,300 for the sensitive, high-yielding variety grown as usual (pp. 51–52). So the margin given up is largest on fresh land. Measured in pots, which the authors would repeat in the field (p. 52). Within the year: the variety is chosen each season.

How far a farm's income follows the price depends on how it sells (World prices of conventional crops). Measured nationally. Within the year, as the harvest is sold.

attributes.description: As harvests get worse, farmers find storing water more worthwhile, and those who can pay for it store more.
attributes.simplification: Folds Relative attractiveness of storing water, which gathered the drivers of this decision: each driver now points at Freshwater storage measures itself, whose description says how farmers weigh storing against their other ways through a dry summer. The attractiveness raised the decision (+), so the link keeps the sign of the step into it and no loop through it changes; the attractiveness was no actor's decision of its own. What it leaves out: whether farmers want to store, apart from whether they can (Farmers' capacity to invest), is no variable on the drawing, only in the description.

attributes.description: Water stored now pays back over years, which suits a farm with a successor.

The attractiveness raised the decision (+), so the link keeps the sign of the step into it and no loop through it changes; the attractiveness was no actor's decision of its own. attributes.description: What a storage measure costs comes out of the money left to invest: its investment in the year it is built, and its upkeep and energy each year it runs. For the island's farms, from a drainage firm's quotes at 2021 prices, anti-salinisation drainage costs about €2,500 a hectare over a life of 15 years, and double drainage €6,000 a hectare to collect the water, with €12,500 to €25,000 for a pump to a basin and €1.80 to €4.00 per m³ for the basin (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 33–34); the creek-ridge infiltration system designed for a cluster of farms on the island's eastern creek ridges, €140,000 to €200,000, written off over about 15 years (p. 50). A year's running costs, figures the study takes from earlier studies, run from €50 for a weir (p. 19) to €1,440 in electricity for a creek-ridge infiltration system (p. 20). The study finds the investment costs high, and for many farms too risky to bear alone (pp. 4–5). Within the year it is built.

The attractiveness raised the decision (+), so the link keeps the sign of the step into it and no loop through it changes; the attractiveness was no actor's decision of its own.

attributes.description: Better tolerant varieties on the market make switching more worthwhile, so more farmers grow them.
attributes.simplification: Folds Relative attractiveness of salt-tolerant varieties, which gathered the drivers of this decision: each driver now points at Adoption of salt-tolerant varieties itself, whose description says that farmers weigh a tolerant variety against the one they grow now. The attractiveness raised the decision (+), so the link keeps the sign of the step into it and no loop through it changes; the attractiveness was no actor's decision of its own.

attributes.description: The more of the current crops' harvest salt takes, the more a new salt-tolerant crop is worth against them, so the more farmers grow it, but only past a threshold: Dutch farmers in salinised areas mostly hold back from saline agriculture unless salt severely hits their production (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 57). In interviews across the salinisation-prone provinces, Zeeland among them, salt in a field was largely invisible and seldom measured, a lower yield hard to put down to salt alone, and the damage not yet significant enough to make it urgent; it would take more dry summers like 2018 (Beauchampet, 2022, p. 216). Nearly all interviewees did not see halophytes as part of the answer, for lack of markets, the soils' intolerance of salt and the hand work they take (p. 221). In Zeeland most farmers still grow the common salt-sensitive crops (van den Burg et al., 2024, p. 6), and on the island the response a source shows is giving up a sensitive crop, sown onions (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 31), not taking up a new one. Years, as farmers come to see the damage over dry summers: a delay.
attributes.simplification: Folds Relative attractiveness of new salt-tolerant crops, which gathered the drivers of this decision: each driver now points at Adoption of new salt-tolerant crops itself, whose description says that farmers weigh a new crop against their current crops. The attractiveness raised the decision (+), so the link keeps the sign of the step into it and no loop through it changes; the attractiveness was no actor's decision of its own. What it leaves out: whether farmers want to switch, apart from whether they can (Farmers' capacity to invest), is no variable on the drawing, only in the description. Folds Farmers' experience of damage, a stock that builds over dry summers, into this link's delay: farmers respond to the damage they come to notice, not to the state of the soil. Every loop through the link keeps its polarity and its mechanism, and the delay is kept; what it leaves out is how far what farmers notice differs from what salt takes.

attributes.description: A better price after transport makes a new crop more worthwhile against the current crops, so more farmers grow it. In France, farmers' low interest in pulses was put down to prices not high enough against major crops such as wheat, and outlets of higher value are needed to give them a reason to grow them (Magrini et al., 2018, pp. 8–9); a premium to farmers doubled the area of pulses within a year, and it fell back the next, buyers downstream not interested in them (Meynard et al., 2018, p. 10); in the Netherlands' salinising provinces, Zeeland among them, nearly all interviewees did not see halophytes as part of the answer, mostly for lack of markets (Beauchampet, 2022, p. 221). In the Netherlands, interviews on quinoa and seed potatoes on saline soil found the lack of economic benefits the main constraint on scaling them (de Wit et al., 2022, p. 276). Within the year: the crop is chosen each season.

attributes.description: Growing a new crop, on their own fields or their neighbours', teaches farmers how.

What a switch costs comes out of the money left to invest, in the year a field changes crop. Switching tends to be costly, its investments weighed against the chance that the new crop pays more than the current one, says a dealer in used machinery for greenhouses and open fields (HortiDaily, 2014), and for Dutch arable farms the investments or the time needed to change their operations leave little room to take on climate and biodiversity (Polman et al., 2026, p. 4). What a switch costs depends on the crop: quinoa is sown with standard equipment and harvested with a combine (van Loo, 2023, p. 75). No source read gives what a switch costs on the island. Within the year.

attributes.description: More harvest within reach makes a plant or chain nearby more worthwhile, so buyers and processors build or keep capacity on or near the island rather than handle the crops elsewhere. In France, the firms that store, process and sell crops specialised in a few dominant ones for economies of scale, so their investment went to those crops and their logistics do not suit minor ones such as pulses (Magrini et al., 2018, pp. 3, 9), and a small volume spread out or far from its users costs more to collect and process (Meynard et al., 2018, pp. 7–8): the economies of scale hold wherever a chain is built, so the mechanism transfers. In the Netherlands, on Terschelling's saline field, producers of processed products are more concerned about volumes than the restaurants are, and stakeholders describe a chicken and egg: a producer needs a market, and a reliable market needs ample supply (ten Dam et al., 2023, pp. 10, 14); for quinoa, one expert says efforts only work with concentrated investments and high volumes (de Wit et al., 2022, p. 270). Years: a Zeeland quinoa chain was a project from 2021 to 2024 (De Vriend, 2024a): a delay.

The attractiveness raised the decision (+), so the link keeps the sign of the step into it and no loop through it changes; the attractiveness was no actor's decision of its own.

attributes.description: A plant or chain nearby takes the harvest at less cost to move and store it, so more of the price reaches the farmer. In France, minor crops grown far from their processor cost much to collect for their volume, collectors building a chain for a crop paid farmers a premium to deliver to its silo, and those without storage suited to small batches sold them fast, below the best price (Meynard et al., 2018, p. 7): the cost of moving and storing a harvest rises with distance and falls with volume wherever a chain runs, so the mechanism transfers. No source read gives what farmers on the island are paid. Within the year: the price is set each season or contract.

That more processing elsewhere raises that price, by processors competing for the harvest or by a plant nearer the island, no source read shows. Within the year: the price is set each season or contract.

attributes.description: Growing the current crops year after year builds up know-how in growing, storing and selling them, and that know-how is of little use for a new crop.
attributes.simplification: Folds Know-how of the current crops, a stock between the two: growing the current crops builds know-how, which is of little use for a new crop. The sign is the product of the two steps (+, then +), so no loop through the link changes, and know-how is no actor's decision. What one link leaves out: the know-how as a stock of its own, built up over years of growing the crops.

attributes.description: The more a farm owns that only its current crops can use, the more a switch leaves idle: a store still stands when its crops take a smaller part of the rotation, and its costs do not fall (Polman et al., 2026, pp. 15, 17), and expensive machines are in some cases suited to one or a few crops (Bonnet & Tiktak, 2025, p. 45). What a new crop can use is not lost (Capital lost on switching). Within the year, at the moment of switching.

attributes.description: What a farm's capital would stop earning holds it to its current crops. Of four arable farmers interviewed about a scheme for less intensive rotations, one, in the loess of Limburg, had recently built a store, which stands and which they want to use, and they and a farmer with plans for water storage said the investment has to be used, so that the onions stored, for example, would not soon leave the rotation (Dijkshoorn-Dekker et al., 2024, pp. 57, 71). Investments in expensive machines suited to one or a few crops keep a contractor and a farmer dependent on those crops for a long time (Bonnet & Tiktak, 2025, p. 45). It holds while the crops can be grown: in the island's low polders, where the surface water is salty all year, farmers have stopped growing sensitive crops such as sown onions (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 31). Within the year, as the rotation is chosen each season.

attributes.description: Money left to invest can go to carrying on: wells, irrigation, drains, a new harvester.

The more of the rotation is potatoes and onions, the more a farm spends on what they need: in farm accounts across the Netherlands from 2014 to 2022 a larger share of ware potatoes, seed potatoes, onions and winter carrots goes with significantly higher costs that no crop is charged with, buildings and machines among them, and storing these crops takes a store (Polman et al., 2026, pp. 5, 11, 15). In France, specialising in a few crops is explained in part by writing off the equipment (Magrini et al., 2018, p. 3). The differences lie mostly between farms, far less in how one farm changes over the years (Polman et al., 2026, p. 4): a farm buys only as a machine or a store falls due, about 12 years for a machine and 33 for a building (Janssens et al., 2020, p. 13). Years, so a delay.

attributes.description: Spending adds to this capital as far as it buys machines and stores for the current crops, not wells or drains: on Dutch arable farms the main category of investment is machines, implements and installations (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19, from national farm accounts), and a store for long keeping is a mostly insulated building with a cooling installation (Janssens et al., 2020, p. 5).

attributes.description: A farm pumps groundwater only through a well it has paid for: in Zeeland extraction is allowed only with horizontal wells, from fresh water more than 15 m thick, outside vulnerable areas (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 26); on the island's eastern creek ridges some arable farmers have laid a deep drain to take water from the ridge (p. 38) and a livestock farmer irrigates from two (pp. 40, 43), and a horizontal well costs €25,000 to €40,000 (p. 49). Within the year, once the well is in.
attributes.simplification: Stands for the whole effect on pumping of a farm's dependence on its current crops, the direct link from Dependence on high-margin salt-sensitive crops folded into this chain: the high-value crops' need for water in a dry spell is in words here. The sign is the chain's (+, then +), so no loop changes its polarity. What it leaves out: a farm that already has wells can irrigate more of a thirsty crop within the year, while the chain runs through the delay on Dependence on high-margin salt-sensitive crops → Spending on keeping the current crops.

attributes.description: A farm with less equity against its debt is a riskier loan: a high solvency can let a farm borrow more and at a lower rate (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19), and more financing still requires a contribution of the farm's own (Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, p. 3). Dutch banks assess investment plans by cash flows, solvency rates and the entrepreneur's track record (van der Meulen & van Asseldonk, 2017, p. 2), and a Rabobank adviser holds that a farm may be expected to have a solvency of at least 30 or 40% (Banken.nl, 2019). Banks weigh it beside the farm's cash flow, which counts more and more (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19). Within the year: a bank judges it with each loan.

attributes.description: A public plan that may change what a farm can earn enters its bank's assessment before the plan is decided. After the government announced its nitrogen plans in June 2022 (Rabobank, 2025, p. 246), a significant part of Rabobank's loans to livestock farmers migrated to stage 2, where the bank places the exposures it considers to have a significant increase in credit risk, which it called also a reflection of the high level of uncertainty (Rabobank, 2023, p. 62); in 2024 it still held an adjustment of 23 million euro to its expected credit losses for the uncertainty the plans left, scoring livestock farmers on the profitability and sustainability of their business model (Rabobank, 2025, p. 246), and its lending criteria include a farm's nearness to a Natura 2000 area (p. 83). Measured for the nitrogen plans and livestock farms across the Netherlands; no source read shows a bank weighing a water level plan, and the mechanism transfers by the bank's test, whether the farm will keep earning enough to meet its obligations, which it applies to every farm loan (Farm income → Banks' risk assessment of farm loans). Within the year: the bank updates its vulnerable sectors at least every half-year (Rabobank, 2023, p. 62).
attributes.sources:

Rabobank. (2025). Annual report 2024. https://vpr.hkma.gov.hk/statics/assets/doc/100197/ar_24/ar_24_eng.pdf

attributes.description: Banks lend less to farms they see as riskier: they have become more critical in lending, counting farm loans riskier despite the land as security (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 47), and hold back on investments not yet proven to pay (p. 8); Dutch farms' bank loans have fallen slightly in recent years, partly through the stricter rules (p. 19). Rabobank, which finances about 85% of Dutch farmers, says that since 2012, in a riskier world, it has often limited the level of financing on farms, and that a farm should be able to bridge two bad years without the bank (Banken.nl, 2019). What the bank charges for the risk is Risk premium on farm loans. Within the year: a bank decides on a loan when it is asked.

attributes.description: Banks charge more for loans they see as riskier: the expected losses and the capital held against a loan, which the premium covers, rise with the credit risk the bank sees in the farm's creditworthiness, the size of the loan, its security and the sector's prospects (ABN AMRO, n.d.-a), and within the terms agreed a bank can change the premium during the loan when the farm's creditworthiness changes (n.d.-b). Within the year: the bank sets the premium with each loan and can revise it during the loan.

attributes.description: Credit is part of what a farm can invest: less room for financing leaves less room to invest in developing the farm and in sustainability (van der Meulen et al., 2020, pp. 47–48), and a farm short of cash asks its bank to defer interest and repayments or for more credit (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 28). Within the year: credit granted is capacity at once.

attributes.description: A new loan adds to a farm's debt while its equity stays the same, so its debt rises relative to its assets and its solvency, equity as a percentage of total capital, falls (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19). Refinancing replaces a loan and adds no debt: the link counts the new money. Farms that expanded in recent years have a lower solvency (Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, p. 3); Dutch farmers under 45 had 68% in 2018 against 76% for those over 65, their higher long-term debt going partly with taking over the farm (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 26); on dairy farms heavy investment and poor results together took five points off solvency between 2006 and 2015 (Silvis et al., 2017, p. 2). The sign holds with the assets' value unchanged: the debt of Dutch arable farms rose 38% between 2010 and 2022, yet in 2022 it was 28% of their balance sheet, the smallest share in farming, as equity grows mainly through the rising value of the land (CBS, 2024). Less credit slows the debt's rise; the debt itself falls through repayments. Within the year: a loan is on the balance sheet once it is paid out.

attributes.description: More credit, more to pay each year: a farm's financing charges are the interest and commission on its loans and the repayment, the periodic amount that pays a loan back within the agreed term (ABN AMRO, n.d.-a), so each new loan adds its interest and repayment to what the farm pays. Within the year, from the loan's payout.

Within the year where the bank sets or revises the premium: with each new loan, and during a loan within its terms (ABN AMRO, n.d.-b). No source read gives how much of the farms' debt carries a premium the bank can revise.

attributes.description: Interest is a cost that lowers a farm's income. Repayments do not count as a cost, income being revenue minus the costs paid and depreciation, yet what a farm can save comes after them (Verhagen et al., 2018, pp. 21, 23): the link joins the two as one assumption, so that repayments reach what a farm can invest through its income, which keeps every loop's polarity.

attributes.description: A farm with high debt payments keeps its lucrative but salt-sensitive crops to meet them.

With more bank credit more farmland is bought, and with less, less: the land a farm can acquire depends on its income and expected income together with its financing (Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, p. 2); with arable returns swinging, banks want larger buffers, which leave less room to finance land, and with a land loan calculated over at most 30 years with repayment, financing land has grown ever harder, which loosens the tie between owning land and using it, while younger farmers, by Rabobank's account, care less about expanding by purchase and are open to lease (pp. 3–4). The route the other way, a farm refused credit selling up, no source read shows: few Dutch farms go bankrupt, 45 in 2016, most in greenhouse horticulture, and a farm short of cash first saves on its spending and asks its bank to defer interest and repayments or for more credit, the bank weighing its continuity over the long term (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 28). Measured nationally. Within the year: a purchase follows its financing.

attributes.description: A farm with a successor stays with the family; one without ends when its farmer stops, and its land comes onto the market: the number of Dutch farms falls by 2 to 3% a year, mainly as farms end at the change of generation, the lack of a successor among the reasons, and the farmers who downsize or end their farm are the ones who supply the land market (Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, p. 2). Measured nationally. The land changes hands as the farm ends.

attributes.description: Farmers attached to their land sell it later, often only when forced.

Expropriated land passes to the body that expropriates it when a notary's deed of expropriation is entered in the public registers (Omgevingswet, 2026, art. 11.18), which can be drawn up only once the expropriation order and the plan it carries out are irrevocable and the provisional compensation is paid (art. 11.16); on the island, the order for the high-voltage station takes effect only once the court has confirmed it (Gemeente Schouwen-Duiveland, 2026, p. 1). Years, so a delay: in the Krimpenerwaard, under the law before the Omgevingswet, the order of October 2020 left two years before the owners still without an agreement had to be summoned to court, by October 2022 (Kamphorst et al., 2025, pp. 26, 45), and the process of the owners expropriated by the court ran more than 61 months on average (p. 67), with continued use of the land until it was handed over (p. 41).

attributes.description: Land that changes hands leaves arable farming when its next holder does not farm it.

Where arable farming still pays, its holder, present or next, keeps the land arable, while what arable farming earns, not what other uses would bid, sets the land's price. A decade or more: land leaves arable use only when a holder gives it up, and just over 1.5% of Zeeland's farmland is sold in a year (Agricultural land value).

Arable land needs lower ditch levels than grassland or nature. By the water board's rules for its whole area, a water level plan starts from an optimal level for each use and soil, the farmland's derived from the optimal drain depths for farming: for arable farming and horticulture 120 cm below the surface on salt-marsh clay (schorgronden) with no sand within 1.2 m, down to 60 on peat, for permanent grassland as a rule 20 cm less (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 7, 19), and for nature 0 cm as a general starting point, its levels set with the site managers, as Duiveland's analysis applied them to its land-use map of 2018 (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 29). So the more hectares farmed as arable land, the more land whose farmers need low levels, in spring as their soil work allows (2021a, p. 66); how strongly they ask for them, no source read shows (Farmers' demand for deep polder drainage → Water board's plans to raise ditch levels). Within the year: the need goes with the land's use each season, while the land leaves arable use only as it changes hands (Arable land in the polders).

attributes.description: A farm that pays finds a successor more easily.

A draft plan that would leave a field with less drainage depth than its use needs gives its owner reason to expect the land to earn less and so be worth less, before any level changes, and owners concerned that a plan lowers their land's value object to it and ask to be compensated; what the level itself does once it takes effect runs, years later, through Polder drainage depth and Spring workability of the fields to Agricultural land value. Respondents to Friesland's peat meadow programme said the uncertainty it creates for a farm's future value lowers the value of land and buildings before the programme takes effect, the 'planological shadow' (Provincie Fryslân & Wetterskip Fryslân, 2021, pp. 3, 31). In their views on draft level plans owners named that fall: in two peat polders, holding the water board liable or asking for a compensation scheme (Graas, 2021, pp. 5, 24), and calling a plan unacceptable because its burden fell on the farmers, in the value of their land and buildings among others (Hoogheemraadschap van Schieland en de Krimpenerwaard, 2022, pp. 5, 16–17), and in the Tielerwaard, on a raise beside a Natura 2000 area, as already at issue once the buffer zone was set (Waterschap Rivierenland, 2019, p. 8). A water board compensates only damage beyond the normal societal risk, the rest staying, wholly or partly, with the owner (Hoogheemraadschap van Schieland en de Krimpenerwaard, 2022, p. 16; Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 14). Whether and how far land loses value the minister called unclear for the peat meadow areas, the question being whether the yield can stay the same or the farmer can earn a comparable income on the land another way (Minister van Landbouw, Natuur en Voedselkwaliteit, 2021, pp. 2–3). Measured elsewhere, in polders where the level change answers subsidence; it transfers as an owner's response to a plan that would leave a field too wet for its use, as in the Braakman near Terneuzen in 2015, where the island's own water board answered ZLTO, objecting for seven farmers, that some would be left with less than optimal drainage depth or with drains under water in winter, both naming damage, not the land's value (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2015, p. 2). On the island the raises of 2021 were to limit drought damage and give the crops more moisture (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 69; 2021b, p. 53): no view on either plan, as the board summarises them, gave the land's value as a reason, the only ones against a raise naming flooding in extreme rain (2021a, p. 53), as farmers across the salinisation-prone provinces want their levels low against flooding and to work their fields with heavy machinery (Beauchampet, 2022, p. 217), and one submitter on each half asked about holding a higher level locally (2021a, p. 53; 2021b, p. 7). Whether a raise that leaves too little drainage depth would raise this concern on the island, no source read shows, nor objections on this ground to the other bodies' plans. Within the year: the views come in the six weeks a draft lies open (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 17).
attributes.simplification: Folds Owners' concern about their land's value, which gathered the reasons for objecting: a fall in the land's value, and a plan that would lower it, raised landowning farmers' concern, and the concern raised their objections. The sign is the product of the two steps, so B13 keeps its polarity, and the concern was no actor's decision of its own. A tenant's concern, losing the lease, was never part of it. What it leaves out: why owners object is no variable on the drawing, a question for the group model building session.
