attributes.description: Farmers who expect public bodies to keep their commitments object less. In views on draft water plans in peat areas, owners named unreliable government, a hidden agenda and agreements not kept beside their other grounds (Graas, 2021, p. 13; Provincie Fryslân & Wetterskip Fryslân, 2021, pp. 6, 14, 85; Hoogheemraadschap van Schieland en de Krimpenerwaard, 2022, p. 29). In experiments with Dutch students, on a national board advising on carbon dioxide storage, how trustworthy the decision maker seemed explained how far they accepted the decision (Terwel, 2009, pp. 77, 81), and in the United States distrust of risk managers goes with political activism (Slovic, 1993, pp. 675–676). Measured elsewhere; it transfers as an owner's response to a body that plans for their land, whatever the plan's reason. It holds while a farmer still acts on the distrust: a view in Friesland reports 'weinig vertrouwen en veel gelatenheid' (Provincie Fryslân & Wetterskip Fryslân, 2021, p. 7), and one submission has a small group on the island, no longer trusting the Province, starting a pipeline plan of its own (Lases, 2021, p. 2). None of the views on the island's two level plans of 2021, as the board summarises them, named trust (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 53; 2021b, pp. 7–8). Within the year: the views come in the six weeks a draft lies open (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 17).

attributes.description: Farmers attached to their land resist plans for it beyond what it is worth in money.

Hypothesis, with two mechanisms for the group model building session: the conflict over a plan itself may lower trust, and a plan delayed, changed or dropped after objections may teach farmers not to count on the next one. Farmers do name changing plans as a reason to distrust public bodies (Farmers' trust in government), but no source read shows a plan changed because of objections costing trust, and where a body takes up an objection those who objected may trust it more, so the sign is part of the question. Within the year once a plan changes: trust can be destroyed in an instant; its recovery, slower, is in the element.
attributes.simplification: Folds Plans changed or dropped. The sign is the product of the two steps (+, then −), so no loop through the link changes. It assumes that a plan changed after objections costs trust as a plan changed for other reasons does, which no source read shows. The public bodies' decisions on their plans stay drawn, on the links from Objections to land-use plans into Water board's plans to raise ditch levels and Farmland planned for other uses.

attributes.description: Land taken against its owner's wish lowers how far farmers expect public bodies to keep their commitments, the more so where they do not count the purpose as a public interest and where voluntary purchase was promised. Of 14 owners interviewed in the Krimpenerwaard, in a process of 2015–2023 ending in expropriation for nature, most experienced it as negative and named an inequality of power; the municipal council had feared for trust between government and farming (Kamphorst et al., 2025, pp. 10, 15, 55). In interviews across the Netherlands, owners who did not count the plan as a public interest, nature development for one, were more often negative about expropriation in itself than those taken for roads (Holtslag-Broekhof et al., 2016, section Equal Treatment), and the chair of LTO held large-scale use against reliable government, farmers having been told that purchases would be voluntary (Neefjes, 2008, p. 3). It starts before any order, from the possibility of one (Kamphorst et al., 2025, p. 55). No source read measures trust before and after, or on the island, where the purposes used so far are a road and the grid, those owners accept most. A tenant may gain (Adviescommissie Natuurherstel Westerschelde, n.d., p. 11). Within the year: trust can be destroyed in an instant, its recovery, slower, is in the element (Slovic, 1993, p. 677).

attributes.description: Objections delay, change or stop a plan in which the municipality designates farmland for another use, while it is pending; with none pending, they change nothing.
A plan that designates farmland for another use leads its owners and the farmers who work it to object, appeal and lobby against it.

Farmland the plan designates for another use leaves arable farming as the plan is carried out on it: the plan does not end the farming by itself. In the Krimpenerwaard, where the land-use plan designating farmland for nature became irrevocable in October 2021 (Kamphorst et al., 2025, p. 25), most of it was sold to the province, 152 hectares, or exchanged, 59 (p. 41), and 24 owners agreed to turn land into nature themselves, 171 hectares of their own and 274 leased from the province (p. 67), a sale being the most common outcome, closely followed by the owners' own conversion (p. 36); voluntary sale and the owners' own conversion alone had not completed it in earlier periods (p. 10). Years, so a delay: the sales took more than 30 months on average, the owners' own conversion more than 61 (p. 67). Expropriation is drawn apart (Farmland planned for other uses → Expropriation of farmland). Measured for nature in the peat meadows of South Holland; the procedure is national law, and how long it takes on the island no source read gives.

attributes.description: Hypothesis: storing water is a long investment that a change of rules can strand, so the less farmers expect public bodies to keep their commitments on water and land, the less they store. A question for the group model building session.

The board tests each level area's drainage depth against the optimum for its use and soil: where more than 10% of the area is too wet, 10 cm or more short of the optimum, the target level is to be lowered or the discharge's bottlenecks solved, and where less than 10% is, a raise is considered (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 9). On Duiveland four level areas may run a lower target for a while in wet periods, where the fields' drainage and workability need it (2021a, p. 40). Years, so a delay: the test runs as a plan is prepared, which the board does when its evaluation every three years finds a plan no longer current, or once a plan is 17 years old (2025, pp. 16–17).

attributes.description: By the water board's rules the level follows the land's use ("peil volgt functie"): the board adapts it to what an area needs (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 5), reading the use from the current land use and from the uses the municipality's land-use plan designates, with what is expected within about five years (p. 7). A plan starts from the optimal level for each use and soil, nature's set with the site managers (2021a, p. 29), and where nature and farmland share a level area on Duiveland the plan keeps nature's level and proposes linking the farm parcel to the neighbouring, lower area (2021a, p. 61). So the less land is farmed as arable land, the more reason for a raise, whoever asks. Years, so a delay: the board weighs it as it prepares a plan, which it does when its evaluation every three years finds a plan no longer current, or once a plan is 17 years old (2025, pp. 16–17).

attributes.description: The saltier the field, the fewer of the crops most sensitive to salt a farm keeps: on low fields with strong saline seepage on the island, farmers have stopped growing sensitive crops such as sown onions (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 31). Years, so a delay: salt in a field is largely invisible and seldom measured, a lower yield is hard to put down to it, and interviewees expected it to take more dry summers like 2018 to make salt urgent (Beauchampet, 2022, p. 216, interviews in the salinisation-prone provinces, Zeeland among them).
attributes.simplification: Folds Farmers' experience of damage, a stock that builds over dry summers, into this link's delay: farmers respond to the damage they come to notice, not to the state of the soil. Every loop through the link keeps its polarity and its mechanism, and the delay is kept; what it leaves out is how far what farmers notice differs from what the soil shows.

attributes.description: With more fresh water a farm keeps or takes on the crops that need it: on the island's low polders, with more fresh water available the farmer is open to more profitable crops and a more varied rotation (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 30). In Zeeland the area of sown onions halved from 4,705 ha in 2019 to 2,579 ha in 2024, the article naming the dry summers, the poor harvests and the lack of fresh water, four in five arable farmers having none, as farmers preferred less risky crops, while elsewhere the area grew (De Vriend, 2024b, for Zeeland). Years, so a delay: farmers respond to the seasons they have had, and the fall ran over five years of dry summers.

attributes.description: The margin given up is net of what the new crop earns, a margin being revenue minus the crop's variable costs (Cloet et al., 2024, p. 1), so the better a new crop pays the less a farm gives up on each hectare it moves to it. Quinoa, in a study for Flanders, yields about 3 tonnes a hectare, sold at €1,100 a tonne under contract on a market still very small (pp. 2–3). Within the year: the crop is chosen each season.

attributes.description: Banks look more and more at a farm's cash flow, whether its operations earn enough to meet all its financial obligations (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19): the bank judges whether the farmer can generate enough over the longer term for interest and repayment, the expected income being the limiting factor rather than the size of the farm (Farjon et al., 2013, pp. 3–4). Basel IV steers banks further toward profitability and liquidity rather than the value of collateral (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 47). So the less a farm earns, the more risk its bank sees, for owner and tenant alike; for the Netherlands. Within the year.

attributes.label: R1 Salty soil takes in less rain
attributes.description: Salt in the root zone puts sodium on the clay; once fresh water washes the salt out, the soil's structure collapses and recovers only over years. Less rain soaks in, less recharges the rainwater lens, the lens thins over years and saline groundwater comes closer to the roots: more salt. It runs in the low polders. The mechanism was measured after seawater floods; how much sodium the island's seepage puts on its clay, no source read shows. No practice is on it: the salt it adds drives tolerant crops and varieties (B2, B1).

attributes.label: B1 Salt losses move fields to tolerant varieties
attributes.description: The more harvest salt takes, the more a tolerant variety is worth against the one grown now, so more farmers grow it, perhaps only past a threshold. A tolerant variety loses less to salt, so the harvest lost falls. It seeks the loss at which a farmer changes variety, a hypothesis for the group model building session: unlike the move to new crops (B2), no source shows that salt losses move farmers to another variety. Tolerant varieties use the same machines, storage and know-how, so little capital is lost on them (R3). It drives tolerant varieties.

attributes.label: B2 Salt losses move fields to new crops
attributes.description: The more harvest salt takes, the more a new salt-tolerant crop is worth against the current crops, so after the dry summers that bring the damage to notice, and perhaps only past a threshold, more farmers grow it. A field moved no longer has a conventional harvest for salt to take, so the harvest lost falls; the salt stays in the soil. It seeks the loss at which a farmer switches: that farmers hold back until salt severely hits their production rests on sources, what sets each farmer's threshold, through their crops, margins, buyers and bank, is a hypothesis for the group model building session. With B1 and B3 it is a way out of the same salt: switching keeps the land arable, B3 is arable farming ending. It drives new crops.

attributes.label: B3 Land leaving arable use lets levels rise and salt fall
attributes.description: More salt in the root zone takes more of the harvest, income and land value fall, and where arable farming no longer pays for a buyer or successor the land goes to a holder who does not farm it as arable land. With less arable land the water board, whose level follows the land's use, has more reason to raise the ditch levels, over years; seepage falls, the rainwater lens thickens and the salt falls back. It seeks the salt level at which arable farming stops paying for any successor or buyer, set by crop prices, margins and the land market. With B2 and B1 it is a way out of the same salt: those keep the land arable with another crop, this one is arable farming ending, where the current crops stop paying and adapting does not pay or is not chosen. It acts only at that end: while arable farming still pays for someone, land from a farm that stops mostly goes to expanding neighbours and stays arable (Arable land in the polders), and a raise follows only where a whole level area leaves arable use, since where nature and farmland share one the board keeps nature's level and links the farm parcel to a lower area (Arable land in the polders → Water board's plans to raise ditch levels). From salt to a raise takes decades, its slowest steps the land changing hands and the board's plan cycle.

attributes.label: B4 Deep drainage keeps fields workable
attributes.description: Where fields stay too wet to work in spring, farmers ask for low ditch levels and the water board plans fewer raises. The levels stay low, the fields drain and dry sooner, and the wish for lower levels eases. It seeks fields dry enough for heavy machinery in spring: what deep drainage gains a farm, R2 tracing what it costs. By keeping the current crops' spring work possible, it supports carrying on with them rather than adopting a practice.

attributes.label: R2 Debt and deep drainage feed each other through salt
attributes.description: A farm with higher leverage is a riskier loan, so banks charge a higher premium and its debt payments rise. To meet them it keeps its high-margin, salt-sensitive crops, whose spring soil work needs fields that dry early, so farmers ask for low ditch levels and the water board, weighing that against raising them, plans fewer raises. The levels stay low, saline seepage stays higher, the rainwater lens thins over years, salt takes more of the harvest, income and land value fall, and leverage rises. It shows an unintended consequence of the deep drainage in B4: the gain comes within the season, the seepage and salt years later. It holds back new crops through the dependence it keeps up, while the salt it adds pushes towards them (B2, B1).

attributes.label: R3 Capital ties farms to their crops
attributes.description: A farm tied to its current crops spends on keeping them as machines and stores fall due, over years. The more it owns for those crops, the more a switch to a new crop would write off, and what it would lose ties it further to them. It holds back new crops, and leaves tolerant varieties of the current crops nearly untouched.

attributes.label: B5 Pumping relieves the shortfall
attributes.description: As the crop water shortfall grows, farmers pump more fresh groundwater, crops get more water and the shortfall shrinks, within the season. It seeks the water the crop needs, and runs only where a farm has fresh groundwater more than 15 m thick under it, on the creek ridges and dunes; the farmers talked to in the low polders do not irrigate. Where it eases the shortfall it eases the worse harvests that make storing worthwhile (B6), so it can hold storage back.

attributes.label: B6 Farms store water when harvests fall
attributes.description: As harvests get worse, farmers find storing water more worthwhile and those who can pay for it store more. Less winter rain drains away, the rainwater lens thickens over years, crops on that field have more fresh water, the shortfall shrinks and yields recover. It seeks the harvest at which storing stops being worth its cost, which each farmer sets against their other ways through a dry summer. It drives storage, slowly, the lens taking years to respond.

attributes.label: B7 A shortfall brings calls for a supply route
attributes.description: The shorter of water the farms, the more firmly ZLTO asks for a supply route, and the deciding body weighs that call over the years a route takes to decide, pay for and build. A route would carry fresh water to the island, crops would have more to draw on and the shortfall would shrink. None exists, so the loop has not run yet; a study has left open who pays and who would run one. It seeks a shortfall the deciding body finds acceptable. Where it eased the shortfall it would ease the worse harvests that make storing worthwhile (B6).

attributes.label: B8 Pumping rules protect the lens
attributes.description: Under the creek ridges and dunes, the thicker the fresh groundwater, the more pumping the water board's rules allow. Farmers pump within that, and what they pump beyond what the rain puts back thins the lens. It seeks the balance between recharge and extraction on which the board set its limit. It shows an unintended consequence of the pumping in B5: a thinner lens, which reaches crops only through wells, so it comes back only through what the rules allow. For storage on the creek ridges, what infiltration adds to this lens is what wells can pump.

attributes.label: R4 Storage keeps up the income that pays for it
attributes.description: A farm with more left to invest can pay for more storage measures, so less winter rain drains away, more recharges the rainwater lens, the lens thickens over years, crops on that field have more fresh water, the shortfall shrinks, and yield, income and what the farm can invest rise. Run backwards, a farm with little left to invest cannot pay for storage, its water gets scarcer and its income falls further: the financial pressure R2 traces through what farms do, R4 traces through what they cannot do. It runs in the low polders. It drives storage on farms with the means and holds it back on farms without.

attributes.label: R5 Storing teaches how storage works
attributes.description: The more measures are built and monitored on the island, the more its farmers, advisers and contractors know of how storage works there and what it costs, risks and yields, and the readier farmers are to invest. Run backwards, where farms do not invest nothing is learned and no knowledge base forms. It drives storage once measures are built and holds it back while few are. How long this takes, no source read shows.

attributes.label: R6 Falling land value cuts the credit to switch
attributes.description: When farmland loses value, the same mortgage is more debt against the farm's assets, so banks see more risk and lend less. The farm has less to invest and moves fewer fields to new salt-tolerant crops, more of its conventional harvest stays exposed to salt, income falls and the land loses more value. It runs for farms that own their land. It shows an unintended consequence of the banks' response in B9: a bank limits its lending to protect itself, and farms that get less credit adapt less, which lowers the collateral further. It holds back new crops where land loses value and supports them where land keeps it.

attributes.label: B9 Banks lend less as leverage rises
attributes.description: A farm with higher leverage is a riskier loan, so banks lend it less, less new debt is added and its leverage stops rising. It seeks the leverage a bank accepts, and is the banks' intended loop: they limit their exposure. By limiting credit it holds back what a farm can invest in new crops and storage; R6 shows what that can do in turn.

attributes.label: B10 Switching gives up margin
attributes.description: Moving a field to a new salt-tolerant crop gives up the current crop's margin, most on fresh land where the current crops still do well. Income and land value fall, leverage and the bank's risk rise, credit falls and the farm has less to invest, so fewer fields move. It seeks the share of new crops that a farm's income and credit can carry. It shares its chain with R6, where the switch saves harvest instead; a sign cannot say which pulls harder, so that is a question for the group. It holds back new crops.

attributes.label: R7 Growers draw a plant, and a plant draws growers
attributes.description: More hectares under new salt-tolerant crops give more harvest within reach of a plant, which makes a local plant more worthwhile to buyers and processors. A plant nearby cuts transport, farmers keep more of the price, the crop is worth more and more farmers grow it. Run backwards, few hectares leave no reason for a plant and transport keeps the price low. It drives new crops once enough is grown and holds them back while too little is.

attributes.label: B11 The water board raises levels against seepage
attributes.description: Lower ditch levels raise the saline seepage. The water board names the salinisation a concern and aims to keep or enlarge the lenses, so over years more seepage gives it more reason to plan raises; once carried out, the levels rise and the seepage falls. It seeks the fresh water in the soil the board wants to keep; how far seepage weighs against drought in its plans, no source read shows. It touches adoption only through the salt it lowers (B2, B1).

attributes.label: B12 The board tests the drainage depth
attributes.description: The water board tests each level area's drainage depth against the optimum for its use and soil: where little of the area is too wet a raise is considered, where much of it is the target level is lowered or the discharge's bottlenecks solved. Carried out over years, the depth moves back towards that optimum, which the board sets by its own rules. It touches adoption only through the seepage and salt the depth sets.

attributes.label: B13 Objections hold back plans
attributes.description: A plan to raise ditch levels brings objections, appeals and lobbying from landowning farmers who expect it to lower their land's value; whether that is their reason is a question for the group model building session. Objections can delay, change or stop the plan while it is pending, so fewer raises stay planned. It is the objectors' intended loop, protecting their land, and seeks a plan they can accept. It touches adoption only through the levels it holds, and through R8 and R9.

attributes.label: R8 Falling land value brings objections that keep salt high
attributes.description: When farmland loses value, its owners may object harder to the next plan to raise ditch levels; whether they do is a hypothesis for the group model building session, the sign possibly opposite where compensation pays more than the land would fetch. Objections can hold today's level while a plan is pending, and never deepen it. Seepage stays higher, the rainwater lens stays thin, salt takes more of the harvest, income falls and the land loses more value. It shows an unintended consequence of the objections in B13: owners object to protect their land, and the levels held keep up the seepage and salt that lower its value. It touches adoption through the salt it keeps up (B2, B1).

attributes.label: R9 Changed plans erode trust
attributes.description: Objections and appeals delay, change or stop plans after public bodies have announced them. Plans changed or dropped teach farmers not to count on the next one, their trust in government falls, and farmers who trust less object more. The step from objections to trust is a hypothesis for the group model building session; the step from trust back to objections rests on sources. It holds back storage, a long investment that a change of rules can strand, as trust falls.

attributes.label: B14 Expropriation makes the next plan harder
attributes.description: The more farmland the municipality plans for other uses, the more lies within reach of an expropriation order, after the attempt to buy has failed, over years. Expropriation lowers farmers' trust in government, farmers who trust less object more, and objections delay, change or stop the next plan, so less farmland is planned. It shows an unintended consequence of expropriating for a plan: the next plan becomes harder to adopt. It seeks the planned area the island's farmers will accept. The steps through trust rest on sources; that objections lower the farmland planned is a hypothesis for the group model building session. Through the trust it lowers it holds back storage.

maps.name: 01 CLD model
02 Actor Map
03 C1 Salt builds, and farms respond in steps
maps.description: Salt in the root zone damages the soil's structure, less rain soaks in, the rainwater lens thins and more salt reaches the roots, in the low polders (R1). The responses differ in speed and cost: a tolerant variety uses the same machines and needs little capital (B1), a new crop comes after a delay (B2), and over years land leaves arable use (B3). The first two lower what salt takes from the harvest and leave the salt in the soil, so they ease the pressure that leads to the third, the one that lowers the salt, through the higher ditch levels that follow. The order is a reading of the delays and the costs, a hypothesis for the group model building session.

maps.name: 04 C2 Low ditch levels: workable fields now, more demand later
maps.description: Low ditch levels dry the fields sooner, within the season, and the farmers' demand for low levels eases (B4). The same low levels raise saline seepage, the rainwater lens thins over years, salt takes more of the harvest, income and land value fall, debt payments rise and the farm depends more on its high-margin crops, whose spring work needs low levels, so the demand comes back higher (R2). The relief comes first and the extra demand years later, on the same variable. R2 comes back through debt and dependence, not through a wetter field, and the link from debt payments to dependence is a hypothesis for the group model building session.

maps.name: 05 C3 Debt and capital together keep a farm in its crops
maps.description: Debt payments raise a farm's dependence on its high-margin crops (R2), and so does what it would write off on machines and stores if it switched (R3); the link from debt payments is a hypothesis for the group model building session, the one from what a switch would write off rests on sources. Each loop raises the variable that drives the other: more dependence brings more spending on machines and stores for those crops and more demand for low ditch levels, so the two add up. Dependence holds back new crops, so a farm can stay with its current crops while salt, on its own, lowers that dependence over the years.

maps.name: 06 C4 The quick answer to a dry summer goes first
maps.description: Three loops answer one crop water shortfall at three speeds: pumping within the season (B5), storage over the years the rainwater lens takes to thicken (B6), and a supply route after the years it takes to decide, pay for and build, which has not run yet (B7). Whatever eases the shortfall first lowers the pressure for the slower answers. Pumping is tied to what it draws on: under the creek ridges and dunes, the thinner the lens, the less the water board's rules allow (B8). The quick answer and the slow one are largely on different farms: pumping where a thick lens lies under the farm, storage through the rainwater lens in the low polders, where the farmers talked to do not irrigate.

maps.name: 07 C5 Storing: more worthwhile, harder to pay for
maps.description: R4 and B6 share the chain from storage measures through the rainwater lens and the shortfall to the harvest, and part ways there. A worse harvest makes storing more worthwhile to a farmer (B6), and leaves the farm less income and less to invest (R4), so the same harvest pushes storage up and down. Farms with the means store and farms without may not, though they face the same water. Which pull is stronger differs per farm: a sign cannot show it, and the group model building session can test it, both links into storage being hypotheses. It runs in the low polders.

maps.name: 08 C6 Salt losses raise the wish to switch and cut the means
maps.description: The harvest lost to salt makes a new salt-tolerant crop worth more against the current crops, after a delay (B2). The same losses lower income and land value, so a bank sees more risk and lends less and the farm has less to invest in the switch (R6); limiting credit is how the bank keeps its own exposure down (B9). A field that moves saves harvest from salt (R6) and gives up the current crop's margin (B10), most on fresh land, so the salt on the field decides whether the switch adds income or costs it. Which of these is stronger, a sign cannot show.

maps.name: 09 C7 New crops stay stuck or take off
maps.description: With few hectares under a new crop there is little harvest within reach of a plant, no local plant, and transport keeps the net price low (R7), while every field moved gives up the current crop's margin, which income and credit must carry (B10), so adoption stays low. With enough hectares a plant becomes worthwhile, the net price rises and more farmers grow the crop. A higher net price also means less margin given up, by a link outside these two loops, which eases the brake B10 puts on adoption. How many hectares that takes, a sign cannot show.

maps.name: 10 C8 One ditch level between four goals
maps.description: Four balancing loops act on the water board's plans for the same ditch levels, each towards its own goal: fields dry enough for heavy machinery in spring (B4), the fresh water in the soil the board wants to keep (B11), the optimum the board sets for each use and soil (B12), and a plan the objecting owners can accept (B13). The goals cannot all be met at once, so the level settles where those pressures balance. How far seepage weighs against the other goals in the board's plans, no source read shows.

maps.name: 11 C9 Objections to one plan shape the next
maps.description: Objections delay, change or stop a plan, which is what owners object for (B13). Two things follow. The levels held keep up the seepage and salt that lower the land's value, and a lower value may bring more objections (R8). And plans changed or dropped, and expropriation for a plan, lower farmers' trust in government, which may bring more objections to the next plan (R9, B14). Whether objections settle at a plan the owners accept or keep growing is a question for the group model building session, three of its steps being hypotheses: from land value to objections, from objections to trust, and from objections to the farmland planned. The trust it lowers also holds back storage, a long investment that a change of rules can strand.

maps.name: 12 C10 Falling land value: levels held, or land leaving arable
maps.description: The three loops share the chain from the water board's plans through the drainage depth, seepage, the rainwater lens, the salt and the harvest to income and land value, and part ways at land value. As land loses value, leverage and debt lead farmers to ask for low levels (R2) and owners may object harder to raises (R8, a hypothesis), so both keep the levels low and the salt coming. Farmers pump within that, and what they pump beyond what the rain puts back thins the lens. It seeks the balance between recharge and extraction on which the board set its limit. It shows an unintended consequence of the pumping in B5: a thinner lens, which reaches crops only through wells, so it comes back only through what the rules allow. For storage on the creek ridges, what infiltration adds to this lens is what wells can pump.

maps.name: 24 R4 Storage keeps up the income that pays for it
maps.description: A farm with more left to invest can pay for more storage measures, so less winter rain drains away, more recharges the rainwater lens, the lens thickens over years, crops on that field have more fresh water, the shortfall shrinks, and yield, income and what the farm can invest rise. Run backwards, a farm with little left to invest cannot pay for storage, its water gets scarcer and its income falls further: the financial pressure R2 traces through what farms do, R4 traces through what they cannot do. It runs in the low polders. It drives storage on farms with the means and holds it back on farms without.

maps.name: 25 R5 Storing teaches how storage works
maps.description: The more measures are built and monitored on the island, the more its farmers, advisers and contractors know of how storage works there and what it costs, risks and yields, and the readier farmers are to invest. Run backwards, where farms do not invest nothing is learned and no knowledge base forms. It drives storage once measures are built and holds it back while few are. How long this takes, no source read shows.

maps.name: 26 R6 Falling land value cuts the credit to switch
maps.description: When farmland loses value, the same mortgage is more debt against the farm's assets, so banks see more risk and lend less. The farm has less to invest and moves fewer fields to new salt-tolerant crops, more of its conventional harvest stays exposed to salt, income falls and the land loses more value. It runs for farms that own their land. It shows an unintended consequence of the banks' response in B9: a bank limits its lending to protect itself, and farms that get less credit adapt less, which lowers the collateral further. It holds back new crops where land loses value and supports them where land keeps it.

maps.name: 27 B9 Banks lend less as leverage rises
maps.description: A farm with higher leverage is a riskier loan, so banks lend it less, less new debt is added and its leverage stops rising. It seeks the leverage a bank accepts, and is the banks' intended loop: they limit their exposure. By limiting credit it holds back what a farm can invest in new crops and storage; R6 shows what that can do in turn.

maps.name: 28 B10 Switching gives up margin
maps.description: Moving a field to a new salt-tolerant crop gives up the current crop's margin, most on fresh land where the current crops still do well. Income and land value fall, leverage and the bank's risk rise, credit falls and the farm has less to invest, so fewer fields move. It seeks the share of new crops that a farm's income and credit can carry. It shares its chain with R6, where the switch saves harvest instead; a sign cannot say which pulls harder, so that is a question for the group. It holds back new crops.

maps.name: 29 R7 Growers draw a plant, and a plant draws growers
maps.description: More hectares under new salt-tolerant crops give more harvest within reach of a plant, which makes a local plant more worthwhile to buyers and processors. A plant nearby cuts transport, farmers keep more of the price, the crop is worth more and more farmers grow it. Run backwards, few hectares leave no reason for a plant and transport keeps the price low. It drives new crops once enough is grown and holds them back while too little is.

maps.name: 30 B11 The water board raises levels against seepage
maps.description: Lower ditch levels raise the saline seepage. The water board names the salinisation a concern and aims to keep or enlarge the lenses, so over years more seepage gives it more reason to plan raises; once carried out, the levels rise and the seepage falls. It seeks the fresh water in the soil the board wants to keep; how far seepage weighs against drought in its plans, no source read shows. It touches adoption only through the salt it lowers (B2, B1).

maps.name: 31 B12 The board tests the drainage depth
maps.description: The water board tests each level area's drainage depth against the optimum for its use and soil: where little of the area is too wet a raise is considered, where much of it is the target level is lowered or the discharge's bottlenecks solved. Carried out over years, the depth moves back towards that optimum, which the board sets by its own rules. It touches adoption only through the seepage and salt the depth sets.

maps.name: 32 B13 Objections hold back plans
maps.description: A plan to raise ditch levels brings objections, appeals and lobbying from landowning farmers who expect it to lower their land's value; whether that is their reason is a question for the group model building session. Objections can delay, change or stop the plan while it is pending, so fewer raises stay planned. It is the objectors' intended loop, protecting their land, and seeks a plan they can accept. It touches adoption only through the levels it holds, and through R8 and R9.

maps.name: 33 R8 Falling land value brings objections that keep salt high
maps.description: When farmland loses value, its owners may object harder to the next plan to raise ditch levels; whether they do is a hypothesis for the group model building session, the sign possibly opposite where compensation pays more than the land would fetch. Objections can hold today's level while a plan is pending, and never deepen it. Seepage stays higher, the rainwater lens stays thin, salt takes more of the harvest, income falls and the land loses more value. It shows an unintended consequence of the objections in B13: owners object to protect their land, and the levels held keep up the seepage and salt that lower its value. It touches adoption through the salt it keeps up (B2, B1).

maps.name: 34 R9 Changed plans erode trust
maps.description: Objections and appeals delay, change or stop plans after public bodies have announced them. Plans changed or dropped teach farmers not to count on the next one, their trust in government falls, and farmers who trust less object more. The step from objections to trust is a hypothesis for the group model building session; the step from trust back to objections rests on sources. It holds back storage, a long investment that a change of rules can strand, as trust falls.

maps.name: 35 B14 Expropriation makes the next plan harder
maps.description: The more farmland the municipality plans for other uses, the more lies within reach of an expropriation order, after the attempt to buy has failed, over years. Expropriation lowers farmers' trust in government, farmers who trust less object more, and objections delay, change or stop the next plan, so less farmland is planned. It shows an unintended consequence of expropriating for a plan: the next plan becomes harder to adopt. It seeks the planned area the island's farmers will accept. The steps through trust rest on sources; that objections lower the farmland planned is a hypothesis for the group model building session. Through the trust it lowers it holds back storage.
